text: Kikukawa Eizan studied first with his father Eiji, a minor painter of the Kanō school, and then with Suzuki Nanrei of the Shijō school. He may also have studied with Totoya Hokkei. In the 1830s he produced many woodblock prints of beautiful women, then gave up printmaking for painting. He was the most prolific, longest-lived and ultimately the best of the late followers of Utamaro who tried to carry on his bijin style. Do not confuse him with Harukawa Eizan.

By the later 15th century Rogier van der Weyden had eclipsed Jan van Eyck in popularity. His paintings were exported to Italy and Spain, and he took commissions from Philip the Good and other Burgundian nobles and foreign aristocrats. His surviving works are mainly religious triptychs and altarpieces, plus portraits and diptychs. He began as Roger de la Pasture. His fame lasted until the 17th century. By the mid-18th century he was almost forgotten.

Jan Bulthuis came from Groningen, where he trained under Jurriaan Andriessen as a painter and Johannes Wieringa as a draftsman. He painted landscapes at first, but later concentrated on townscapes and country views. From 1780 he worked in Amsterdam. In 1785 he enrolled at the Stadstekenacademie and won a gold medal there. He made a series of drawings for Adriaan Loosjes's description of the Zaan villages. He died in 1801.

Francesco Bassano the Younger studied with his father Jacopo and worked in the family workshop with his three brothers. He was the eldest son. Francesco moved to Venice, where he ran the branch of the family business, and he was commissioned to paint a series of historical pictures in the Doge's Palace. He was prone to hypochondria. That made his other ailments worse. He died in 1592.

Three separate blocks went into every print by Antonio da Trento: one for the outlines, one for the shadows, and one for the lighter tints. He specialized in chiaroscuro woodcuts, mostly of religious subjects. He probably learned wood engraving from Ugo da Carpi, and later followed Parmigianino and then the School of Fontainebleau. Three documented works are The Beheading of St. Peter and St. Paul, The Tiburtine Sibyl and Psyche Saluted by the People.

Jerome Myers worked briefly as an actor and scene painter before studying art for a year at Cooper Union and then eight years at the Art Students League, mainly with George de Forest Brush. Born in Petersburg, Virginia, he spent his adult life in New York City. He painted the city and its people with sympathy. He helped organize the 1913 Armory Show, which introduced European modernism to America. He also wrote.

Hardly any documents mention Hans Brosamer apart from his prints. He was probably born in Fulda in the late 1490s, was active there from 1536 to 1545, and later worked in Erfurt. His works include over 600 woodcuts, mostly book illustrations, and 38 engravings. Because his engravings are small, he counts among the Little Masters. He also painted half-length portraits of local elites. He died around 1554.

Giovanni Battista Vanni studied under Jacopo da Empoli, Aurelio Lomi and Matteo Rosselli, and then became a disciple of Cristofano Allori. He is better known as an engraver than as a painter. From 1624 to 1632 he lived in Rome, and he went back to Florence after visiting Venice. In 1642 he etched fifteen plates after Correggio's frescoes in the cupola of Parma Cathedral. He also engraved Veronese's Marriage at Cana.

At twenty Joseph Vivien left Lyon for Paris and found work in Charles Le Brun's large atelier. In 1701 the Académie royale accepted him as a pastel portraitist, and his reception pieces, pastel portraits of the sculptor François Girardon and the architect Robert de Cotte, are in the Louvre. He was made counsellor to the Academy and housed at the Gobelins. He visited Brussels and worked in Munich as first painter to a brother of the Elector of Cologne.

Adriaan de Lelie came from Tilburg and trained with A. Peeters, who painted ornaments, and then with Andreas Bernardus de Quertenmont in Antwerp. In Düsseldorf he copied many portraits by Rubens and Van Dyck. On Professor Camper's advice he settled in Amsterdam. He painted a great number of portraits and cabinet pictures, including one of the art lover Jan Gildemeester showing his collection to a party. His Drawing Academy of the Felix Meritis Society is one of his best.

In 1846 John Mix Stanley showed a gallery of 85 of his paintings in Cincinnati and Louisville. He grew up in the Finger Lakes region of New York and started by painting signs and portraits. In 1842 he went to the American West to paint Native American life. In the Mexican–American War he joined Colonel Kearney's expedition to California and painted the campaign, and later the Oregon Territory. A big exhibit followed at the Smithsonian. It held over 150 works.

Tawaraya Sōtatsu is best known for decorating calligraphic works by his partner Hon'ami Kōetsu. His folding screens are spectacular and highly influential, and two of them, Wind God and Thunder God, are National Treasures. He also painted the Sekiya and Miotsukushi chapters of The Tale of Genji. He popularized tarashikomi. In that technique a second layer of paint goes on before the first dries. With Kōetsu he is credited with co-founding the Rinpa school.

Pietro della Vecchia was once incorrectly called Pietro Muttoni. He worked in many genres between late Mannerism and early Baroque: altarpieces, portraits, genre scenes and grotesques. He also made pastiches of the leading Italian painters of the 16th century. He designed cartoons for mosaics and restored art, and collectors sought him out as an expert and for valuations of artworks. He lived mostly in Venice.

Very little documentation of Simone Martini's life survives, and art historians debate many attributions. He is thought to have been a pupil of Duccio. Vasari said he was a pupil of Giotto instead, and went with him to Rome. His brother-in-law was the artist Lippo Memmi, and Gombrich said he was a friend of Petrarch. He greatly influenced the International Gothic style. He came from Siena and died in 1344.

Two folding screens by Ogata Kōrin are registered National Treasures: Irises, and Red and White Plum Blossoms. He also decorated round fans, writing boxes and medicine cases. His brother Kenzan made the ceramics and lacquerware that he painted. He is credited with reviving the Rinpa school of painting, fifty years after Hon'ami Kōetsu founded it. He worked as a lacquerer too. He died in 1716.

George Auriol made magazine covers, book illustrations, sheet music, monograms and trademarks, and he also wrote poems and songs. Eugène Grasset introduced him to typography and book design after he arrived in Paris in 1883. Georges Peignot then appointed him to create the Auriol typeface for the Peignot foundry. It was inspired by Art Nouveau. Publishers such as Francis Thibaudeau used it. His real name was Jean-Georges Huyot.

Adam Elsheimer painted small oils on copper, the cabinet paintings, with a variety of light effects and a new way of treating landscape. He had a short career in Rome, and his few works were very influential. Rembrandt and Rubens were among those he influenced. He was one of ten children of a master tailor in Frankfurt. His father's house, near the church that held Dürer's Heller Altarpiece, was destroyed by bombs in 1944. He died in 1610.

Julian Onderdonk is often called the father of Texas painting. His father Robert and his sister Eleanor were painters too. As a teenager in San Antonio he got some training from the Texas artist Verner Moore White. He was an enthusiastic sketcher from boyhood. Onderdonk attended the West Texas Military Academy. He painted Texas Impressionist landscapes and lived from 1882 to 1922.

Jacobus van Looy lost his mother at five, and when his carpenter father died soon after, he ended up in the municipal orphanage in Haarlem. He trained as a house painter but managed to follow drawing classes, from 1877 at the Rijksacademie in Amsterdam. In 1884 he won the Prix de Rome. He then travelled through Italy, Spain and Morocco. He wrote as well as painted.

Giuseppe De Nittis grew up in the wealthiest district of Barletta, near the Corso Vittorio Emanuele, around the corner from the birthplace of the painter Geremia Discanno. He became one of the most important Italian painters of the 19th century. His work merges Salon art with Impressionism. His Paris pictures include the Avenue du Bois de Boulogne and the Arc de Triomphe. He died young, in 1884.

A gamekeeper's son from near Dorfen, Johann Georg von Dillis was educated in Munich with support from the prince-elector of Bavaria. He was trained for the priesthood first, but his real interest was art, and by 1786 he taught drawing at court. In 1790 he became inspector of the Hofgarten Galerie. He kept a curatorial role at the Bavarian court for much of his career, which left him freedom to travel. He first went to Italy in 1794.

At fifteen Jan Adam Kruseman went to Amsterdam and enrolled at the Tekenacademie, where his cousin Cornelis Kruseman gave him his first lessons. He studied in Brussels with François-Joseph Navez and Jacques-Louis David. At twenty-six he became Director of the Academy of Fine Arts. He came from a Haarlem family that produced several well-known artists. He is known mainly for portraits, though he also did landscapes and genre scenes.

Constant Puyo led the Pictorialist movement in France and argued that photography was an artistic medium. He came from a prominent family in Morlaix, and his father Edmond was a painter, amateur archaeologist and mayor in the 1870s. His uncle was the best-selling author Édouard Corbière. For most of his career he was tied to the Photo Club of Paris and served as its president from 1921 to 1926. His photographs appeared in publications worldwide.

Adolf von Becker studied law and drawing at the same time in Helsinki. After he completed his law degree in 1853 he began as a trainee at the Court of Appeals in Turku, still making drawing trips into the countryside. Robert Wilhelm Ekman urged him to study at the Royal Danish Academy of Fine Arts, and he graduated there in 1856. He was one of the first Finnish artists to study in Paris and taught many young artists of the Golden Age of Finnish Art.

Three generations of Protestant pastors came before Johann Friedrich Overbeck in Lübeck, and his father was a burgomaster, poet and mystic. His uncle ran the Gymnasium next to the family mansion. There Johann became a classical scholar and got art lessons. He left in March 1806 for the academy in Vienna under Heinrich Füger. He became a founder of the Nazarene art movement. He died in 1869.

Willem Drost is a mysterious figure, closely linked to Rembrandt, and very few paintings can clearly be attributed to him. He was presumably born in Amsterdam. Houbraken says he studied with Rembrandt and then developed a close working relationship with him. He painted history scenes, biblical compositions, studies of a solitary figure and portraits. His Bathsheba of 1654 was inspired by Rembrandt's. He died young, in 1659.

Theodore Robinson grew up in Evansville, Wisconsin, and briefly studied art in Chicago. In 1874 he went to New York to attend classes at the National Academy of Design. He studied in Paris under Carolus-Duran and Jean-Léon Gérôme, and showed at the 1877 Salon. He visited Giverny and became a close friend of Claude Monet. He was one of the first American artists to take up Impressionism. He died in 1896.

Antonio Visentini, a Venetian, studied under the widely travelled Baroque painter Giovanni Antonio Pellegrini. He made architectural fantasies and capricci, wrote treatises on perspective and was a professor at the Venetian Academy. Today he is best known as the engraver for Canaletto's first great series of Venetian views. The British consul Joseph Smith organized it, and it was begun around 1728 and finished in 1735.

John Opie was the youngest of five children of a master carpenter in Cornwall. By twelve he had mastered Euclid and opened an evening school for poor children. His father did not encourage him and apprenticed him to his own trade of carpentry. But his ability for drawing won out. He became a painter of prominent men and women of his day, including members of the British royal family. He lived from 1761 to 1807.

Nicholas Pocock followed his father to sea and was master of a merchant ship by twenty-six. He became a skilled artist by making ink-and-wash sketches of ships and coastal scenes in his logbooks. In 1778 his employer Richard Champion went bankrupt, hit by the effects of the American Revolutionary War on trade. Pocock gave up the sea and devoted himself to painting. The Royal Academy first exhibited his work in 1782. He specialised in marine art.

A German innkeeper settled in Amsterdam in 1636 with his family, and his son Johannes Lingelbach grew up there. The father ran a labyrinth garden with an astronomical clock and machines that moved or played music and showed biblical or mythological scenes. Johannes lived in Paris from 1642 to 1644, then moved to Lyon, Genoa and Rome. In Rome he worked with several Bentvueghels. He belonged to the second generation of the Bambocciate, genre painters working in Rome.

Haarlem is where Jan Wijnants grew up, the son of a Catholic art dealer who remarried a widow, which made Jan the stepbrother of the painter Egbert van Heemskerck. Jan worked in Haarlem until 1660 and then moved to Amsterdam, where he died. He is mainly known for Italianate landscapes and topographical pictures. Nicolaes de Vree and Adriaen van de Velde trained in his studio. His style later influenced Thomas Gainsborough.

Willy Sluiter came from a family of ministers and grew up in Heerenveen and Zwijndrecht, the son of a notary. He is best known for paintings of Dutch villages and their dwellers. He also painted portraits of Dutch high society, and his work was part of the art competitions at four Olympic Games. He married in 1901 and had a daughter. He lived in Dordrecht and Rotterdam. He died in The Hague.

Ivan Shishkin came from a family of merchants in Yelabuga, and his father traded grain. His grandfather had been a palace peasant who registered as a third-guild merchant in 1792. Shishkin became a Russian Realist painter and draughtsman, best known for landscapes. He was one of the most notable artists to emerge under Tsar Alexander II and one of the founding members of the Peredvizhniki. He lived from 1832 to 1898.
